activity_label: Observe how a small paper setup is used
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional brief: a shared desk needs a place to keep five blank paper slips without blocking a reader’s notebook. Use five scraps of paper, one sheet as a pretend notebook and your own safe desk surface; no actual shared desk or user is being investigated.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Arrange the notebook sheet and five slips as a starting layout. Sketch it, including the edges of your working area. Write what the fictional user needs and what is still unspecified.

Step 2: Move one slip away and put it back three times. Observe paper movement, reach and obstruction. Record only what happens in your own setup; if you cannot try it, mark that observation unperformed.
Step 3: Change just the slip location and repeat the same action. Note which visible detail changed. Do not claim that a person elsewhere would find it easier.
Step 4: Keep the two sketches and one unresolved question. Choose a next observation, such as a different paper size, without buying materials or recruiting participants.

Record and completion: Keep a before/after sketch and a log with arrangement, action, visible result, practical constraint and unknown. Complete the loop when one change has an observation or an explicit unperformed status.

Reflection: Which part did you want to continue: manipulating the setup, noticing movement or understanding how it is used? Would you repeat a less novel observation? Separate limited materials or tiredness from a dislike of the activity.
Boundaries: Use paper on a stable surface. No heavy items, sharp tools, machinery or real workplace access. The fictional brief is not an ergonomic standard or a claim about any occupation.

Optional continuation: Optional: take one additional short round of this same exercise, changing one condition named in your reflection. Keep the two records; do not treat ease or improvement as an interest score. Optional, up to two hours only if useful: develop this same small output with materials already available. Fictional brief: hold the cards inside a 10-centimetre square and remove one without pulling the others out. These dimensions are exercise constraints, not a product standard. Use materials already available; otherwise mark construction unperformed.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Step 2: Build one rough paper model. Load the ten cards and remove one card three times, noting slipping, collapse or unintended movement. Keep a failed attempt as usable observation.
Step 3: Change one main factor, such as base width, fold angle or an edge. Repeat the same three attempts, retaining both versions or their sketches.
Step 4: Explain what you kept, rejected and have not checked. A problem statement, two sketches, a model and observations tied to a change complete the exercise even if the model still fails.

activity_label: Trace a paper setup problem one change at a time
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional observation card: “A paper holder moved when a card was removed. The desk surface and pulling direction were not recorded.” Reuse your IAR paper model if available, or fold a single scrap of paper into a holder for three blank slips. The observation card is invented, not a report of your trial.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Copy the fictional observation separately from anything you actually observe. List two possible explanations, such as how the holder rests or the direction of the pull; label them guesses.
Step 2: If you have a safe paper setup, repeat one removal and describe it without explaining the cause. Otherwise sketch the proposed observation and mark it unperformed.
Step 3: Change only one arrangement detail and repeat. A change that coincides with different movement does not settle the cause; record other uncontrolled details.
Step 4: Write one next check and one stopping condition. Stop after one comparison or when the setup cannot be tried safely; an unresolved cause is an acceptable completion.

Record and completion: Make columns for initial condition, observed action, possible explanation, single change, observed result and unresolved factors. Keep fictional and actual entries explicitly separated.
Reflection: Did you want to keep tracing the cause, or only finish fixing the object? Which uncertainty was interesting and which was frustrating? What condition would you change before another try?
Boundaries: Paper only: no dismantling devices, batteries, mains power, heat or moving mechanisms. This is not fault-finding certification or proof of technical ability.

activity_label: Turn a broad question into an observable question
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional note: “The desk is always confusing. A slip was hard to find on Monday, four slips were found quickly on Tuesday, and nobody recorded where the slips were placed.” The days and events are invented. Use this note and a blank sheet.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Underline observations, evaluative words and missing information using three labels rather than relying on colour. Do not upgrade “always confusing” into a measured fact.

Step 2: Write a narrower question that names an action and a condition: for example, what happens when the slips have one labelled place? List what “hard to find” would need to mean in an observation.
Step 3: Draw a small observation plan with the same item set and one layout change. State what you would record and what this small plan would not establish.
Step 4: Rewrite the question once after finding a missing condition. Keep both versions and one alternative question rather than forcing a single correct formulation.
Record and completion: Keep a known/unknown/assumption list, two versions of the question and a proposed observation. No experiment or fictional observation becomes a measured personal result.

Reflection: Which part made you curious: defining words, isolating a condition or designing an observation? Would you want to investigate the revised question? Note if the topic itself was uninteresting.

activity_label: Compare what three fictional notes can support
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Three invented source cards concern a paper holder. Card A, an observation note: “With ten cards, the base moved during one removal; pull direction not recorded.” Card B, a material note: “This model used thin paper; no comparison with thick card.” Card C, a comment: “I like the appearance; I did not try removing a card.” None is an external research source.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write a question: what do these notes tell us about using the holder? Keep the three source labels and their exact stated limitations.
Step 2: For each card, record the claim it supports and one claim it cannot support. Appearance approval cannot establish ease of removal; a single movement cannot explain its cause.
Step 3: Place one apparent disagreement side by side. Decide whether it is a real contradiction or concerns different aspects. Mark missing corroboration instead of counting notes as votes.
Step 4: Write a cautious two-sentence account and the next evidence you would want. Do not search for people, buy materials or claim that the invented cards establish real product facts.
Record and completion: Produce a three-row evidence table: source card, observation or opinion, supported statement, limit and next evidence. Retain “unknown” when no card answers the question.
Reflection: Did comparing scope and uncertainty make you want to examine another source? Did you prefer resolving the question quickly? Keep that response separate from the quality of your summary.

activity_label: Plan a check that could challenge an explanation
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional log: “A paper holder moved in one trial with ten cards and stayed still in another with five. Pull direction and base arrangement were not controlled.” This is invented, not an experimental finding.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write two possible explanations that could account for the note. For each, name an observation that would be consistent with it and one that would make you question it.
Step 2: Design one safe comparison using only paper materials: keep one proposed condition fixed and change one other. State which details remain uncontrolled.

Step 3: Write predicted observations as “if this explanation is useful, I might see…” without filling in a result. Running the comparison is optional; any real observation must be separately labelled.
Step 4: Review whether both explanations still could hold. Keep an unresolved alternative and a next check; do not treat a single small comparison as proof.

Step 2: Write a second description that makes the same room feel uncertain, then a third that makes it feel ordinary. Keep object facts consistent; frame invented details as part of fiction.

activity_label: Write a scene, then change its ending
task_examples: Materials and fictional brief: Fictional prompt: “An empty chair remains beside a table after a small gathering. A blue ribbon lies on the seat. Someone returns to the room.” Invent the people and their reasons; use no identifiable real experience.

Scope and conditions: Use only your own non-sensitive materials or the supplied fiction. No paid tool, account, outside contact or public posting is required. A willing partner already present is optional except where live interaction is explicitly needed; solo preparation never counts as another person’s feedback. Stop or pause at any point. Timing is a flexible planning aid, not a performance limit.
Step 1: Write a five-sentence scene with an opening action, a concrete detail, a change, a response and an ending. These are prompts, not a marking rubric.
Step 2: Underline one detail that shapes how you imagine the scene. Write a different opening or ending while keeping the ribbon and chair in the scene.

activity_label: Check two records and keep uncertainty visible
task_examples: Materials: use paper or a plain table. All amounts are pieces. List A / List B: Blue pens 8 / 6; Pencils 5 / 5; Rulers 3 / 4; Paper clips 12 / not recorded; Markers 2 / 2. Both lists are fictional and unverified; not recorded means unknown, not zero. Do not use personal, employer or customer records.

Purpose and rule, about 5 minutes: keep both originals unchanged. Make columns for item, A, B, comparison status, evidence, unanswered question and next check. Mark equal entries as entries agree, actual stock unverified; different entries as entries differ, reason unknown; missing entries as unknown, confirmation needed.

Check, about 6 minutes: compare the same item and unit in all five rows. For blue pens, write A says 8 and B says 6, without inferring loss. For paper clips, preserve 12 in A and not recorded in B. Choose one unresolved row and describe evidence that could resolve it. A real recount is not available in this fictional exercise; do not invent one or contact anyone.

Review, about 4 minutes: note the part you wanted to continue or avoid, the conditions that affected the experience, and one condition to change next time. Choose repeat, change a condition or stop for now. Finish when every row has a comparison status and one unresolved row has a proposed verification step. Do not calculate an accuracy or interest score.

Record: keep the log and choose your own next-trial and review dates. Existing personal-note fields may hold the task, conditions and next trial; Career evidence should say no occupation investigated, role-specific facts unknown. These notes stay in page memory; manually copy what you want before leaving or refreshing. This exercise supplies no automatic save or export.

Optional continuations of the same task: at about 30 minutes, clarify a rule and try a fresh fictional list; for up to 2 hours if useful, compare dated counts of a few of your own non-sensitive household supplies; during one week, repeat twice while changing one condition. Stop after one loop if that is enough. No outside contact, spending or paid tool is required.

Interpretation: observe willingness to repeat and contextual effort separately from performance. Keep alternative interests open when results are close or broad. Do not change measured scores or codes, compare numeric changes between the 60- and 140-item forms, or infer skills, qualifications, job fit or hiring outcomes from the exercise.
